title: Surface supported-cohomology presentation and flag representatives
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime, $n\geq1$, $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, and $S$ a Noetherian excellent normal integral strictly henselian local scheme of dimension $2$, with closed point $s$ and $\ell$ invertible [def-exc-excellent-ring, def-weil-pbc-normal-ring, def-pc-integral-scheme, def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology, def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Use ordinary etale cohomology and closed supports [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories, def-pur-etale-derived-supported-sections], and the twists and immediate transitions of [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex]. There exists a projective birational morphism $p:S'\to S$, an isomorphism away from $s$, with $S'$ regular and $E=p^{-1}(s)_{\mathrm{red}}$ a strict normal-crossing union of regular proper curves $D_1,\ldots,D_N$, $N\geq1$ [def-weil-proper-morphism, def-weil-regular-scheme]. The intersection graph of these curves is connected. A strict normal crossing here means that at most two components pass through a point and that at an intersection they are defined by the two elements of a regular system of parameters [def-weil-pbc-regular-system-of-parameters]. There are canonical maps giving an exact sequence
$$\bigoplus_{i<j}\ \bigoplus_{z\in D_i\cap D_j}\Lambda\xrightarrow{\partial}\bigoplus_{i=1}^N\Lambda e_i\xrightarrow{\epsilon}H^4_s(S,\Lambda(2))\longrightarrow0,$$
where $\partial(e_z)=[\kappa(z):\kappa(s)](e_i-e_j)$; all these residue degrees are invertible in $\Lambda$. Under $H^4_s(S,\Lambda(2))\cong H^4_E(S',\Lambda(2))$, $\epsilon(e_i)$ is the enlargement of support of $[\kappa(z):\kappa(s)]^{-1}\operatorname{Cl}_{z\hookrightarrow S'}$ for any closed point $z\in D_i$, where $\operatorname{Cl}$ is the regular Gysin class [lem-per-absolute-gysin-purity].
For any codimension-one point $y$ of $S$, one can choose such a resolution on which the strict transform of its reduced closure is its normalized strictly henselian trait. If it meets $E$ at $z\in D_i$, then the composite of the two normalized immediate transitions along any geometric flag $\bar\eta\rightsquigarrow\bar y\rightsquigarrow\bar s$ sends $1$ to $\epsilon(e_i)$. Any two such resolutions admit a common dominating resolution. Each dominating morphism is an isomorphism over an open of the target whose complement has dimension zero, so this open meets an exceptional component in a nonempty open containing a closed point. For a morphism between two of them that is an isomorphism over a closed point of the exceptional curves, pullback identifies the normalized point Gysin classes and hence their enlargements of support.

source.place: Expose XVII sections 3.4.1–3.4.3: existence of an SNC resolution, Propositions 3.4.1.1(d), 3.4.1.2–3.4.1.3, the connectedness observation in 3.4.1.4, common domination in 3.4.2, and the normalized support square of Lemma 3.4.3.1; printed pp.270–274

proof.text: Apply the surface-resolution theorem to $S$. Its normal local rings at height one are DVRs, so its punctured spectrum $U=S-\{s\}$ is regular. The resolution is therefore an isomorphism over $U$. Apply embedded resolution to the closed fibre in the resulting regular excellent surface. If the first resolution is the identity, this operation includes blowing up $s$, so the reduced fibre is a nonempty divisor, rather than a point. All centres lie over $s$. The resulting projective birational $p:S'\to S$ is still an isomorphism over $U$, and its reduced fibre is an SNC union of finitely many regular curves. These curves are proper over $\kappa(s)$, since $p$ is proper and they are closed in its fibre. Excellence and Noetherianity of the finite-type models and their localizations follow from the cited stability lemma. Projectivity of the successive composites follows from H-projective composition. The affine base has ample $\mathcal O_S$: principal affine opens form a basis.

source.place: XVII §3.4.1, SNC resolution preparation, printed pp.270–271

proof.text: The proper morphism $p$ has integral reduced source, normal integral target, and generic fibre $\operatorname{Spec}k(S)$. Thus its generic global functions equal $k(S)$ as required by the geometric-connectedness theorem. Its closed fibre is geometrically connected and nonempty. Reduction does not change its underlying space. If the intersection graph of the finitely many $D_i$ were disconnected, partition its vertices into two nonempty parts without an edge between them. The corresponding two finite unions of closed components would be disjoint closed subsets covering $E$, hence also open; this contradicts connectedness. Thus the graph is connected.

Every $D_i\cap D_j$ is zero dimensional because the curves are distinct components of an SNC divisor. Its finite-type structure over $k=\kappa(s)$ makes it finite over $k$. In an SNC chart its ideal is generated by a regular system of parameters, so this intersection is reduced and regular. Each closed point of any $D_i$ has finite residue degree over $k$ by Zariski's lemma applied on an affine neighbourhood. The field $k$ is separably closed. Its finite residue extensions are purely inseparable, hence their degrees are powers of the residue characteristic (or $1$ in characteristic zero), and are units modulo $\ell^n$. Such residue fields are separably closed too: an element separable over a purely inseparable algebraic extension is separable over the base after a sufficiently large characteristic-power, and so already lies in that extension.

source.place: XVII Propositions 3.4.1.2–3.4.1.4, intersection points and invertible degrees

proof.text: The strictly henselian acyclicity theorem gives $H^q(S,\Lambda(2))=0$ for $q>0$. Proper base change for $p$, evaluated at the geometric closed point, and the strict-local global exchange identify restriction $H^q(S',\Lambda(2))\to H^q(p^{-1}s,\Lambda(2))$ with an isomorphism. The fibre has dimension one over the separably closed field $k$; the finite-type torsion cohomological-dimension bound gives vanishing for $q>2$. Apply the functorial localization sequences to $(S,s)$ and $(S',E)$ with the common complement $U$. Both boundary maps from $H^3(U,\Lambda(2))$ to their fourth supported groups are isomorphisms. Their naturality gives the claimed canonical pullback $H^4_s(S,\Lambda(2))\xrightarrow{\sim}H^4_E(S',\Lambda(2))$.

For a closed reduced subset $F\subseteq S'$ put $A_F=(i_F)_*\Lambda_F$. The restriction maps give a short exact sequence $0\to A_E\to\bigoplus_i A_{D_i}\to\bigoplus_{i<j}A_{D_i\cap D_j}\to0$, whose last map at an intersection is $(a_i,a_j)\mapsto a_i-a_j$. Indeed a geometric point outside $E$ gives the zero sequence, a point of exactly one component gives the identity sequence, and a crossing gives $0\to\Lambda\xrightarrow{a\mapsto(a,a)}\Lambda^2\xrightarrow{(a,b)\mapsto a-b}\Lambda\to0$. Kernels and cokernels can be checked on exact conservative geometric stalks. Here the direction of the displayed sheaf sequence in the printed proof of 3.4.1.2 is reversed; the restriction sequence above is the exact one and yields the printed supported-cohomology sequence after contravariant Hom. The closed-pushforward stalk formula gives these stalks on the closed subset; outside it the complementary open neighbourhood has empty inverse image and hence zero sections.

source.place: XVII Proposition 3.4.1.2, corrected direction of the displayed sheaf restriction sequence

proof.text: Take the distinguished triangle of that short exact sequence and apply contravariant $\operatorname{Hom}(-,\Lambda(2)[q])$. The closed-support Hom identification identifies the terms with supported cohomology. The resulting exact segment is $\bigoplus_{i<j}H^4_{D_i\cap D_j}\to\bigoplus_i H^4_{D_i}\to H^4_E\to\bigoplus_{i<j}H^5_{D_i\cap D_j}$. Finite direct sums require no interchange of infinite limits. Purity for the regular codimension-two closed immersions identifies each final summand with $H^1(D_i\cap D_j,\Lambda)$. It is zero by the separably closed zero-dimensional affine acyclicity theorem, using step 3. Thus the first three terms form a right exact sequence; its maps are enlargement of support and their differences, with the sign fixed in step 5.

source.place: XVII Proposition 3.4.1.2, derived Hom and vanishing

proof.text: For each regular divisor $D_i\hookrightarrow S'$, apply regular-pair purity, which permits nonaffine schemes, to identify $H^4_{D_i}(S',\Lambda(2))$ with $H^2(D_i,\Lambda(1))$. The curve trace identifies this group with $\Lambda e_i$. Similarly purity identifies $H^4_{D_i\cap D_j}$ with one copy of $\Lambda$ for each intersection point. Composition of regular-immersion Gysin classes identifies enlargement from a point $z$ into $D_i$ and then $S'$ with the point class in $S'$. Its trace on $D_i$ is $[\kappa(z):k]$. Hence the two coordinates of the difference map are exactly $[\kappa(z):k]e_i$ and $-[\kappa(z):k]e_j$. Substituting these identifications into step 6 gives the asserted presentation and differential.

Here $\operatorname{Cl}_{z\hookrightarrow S'}$ is the absolute-purity class of the statement, while steps 6--7 and the curve trace use the Kummer-normalized classes $\eta$; they agree. Since $\mathcal O_{S',z}$ and $\mathcal O_{D_i,z}$ are regular local of dimensions $2$ and $1$, after shrinking there is an affine open $W\ni z$ of $S'$ with $D_i\cap W=V(f)$ and $\{z\}=V(g)$ in $D_i\cap W$. The support-restriction triangle with $B=\{z\}$ and $C=S'-W$, $B\cap C=\varnothing$, identifies $H^4_z(S',\Lambda(2))$ with $H^4_z(W,\Lambda(2))$. Both $z\hookrightarrow D_i\cap W$ and $D_i\cap W\hookrightarrow W$ are regular principal Cartier divisors in affine excellent regular schemes, so the Cartier-Gysin normalization gives $\operatorname{Cl}(1)[2]=\eta$ for each. The composition clauses of absolute purity and of the regular-immersion class calculus give $\operatorname{Cl}_{z\hookrightarrow W}(2)[4]=\eta_{z\hookrightarrow W,n}$. For any closed $z\in D_i$, composition of Gysin classes and the trace formula give that $[\kappa(z):k]^{-1}\operatorname{Cl}_{z\hookrightarrow S'}$ enlarges in $H^4_{D_i}$ to $e_i$. Thus its further enlargement to $E$ is $\epsilon(e_i)$, independently of $z$. The coefficient is a unit by step 3. Since the graph is connected and every edge coefficient is a unit, the presentation also shows that all $\epsilon(e_i)$ coincide: across an edge their difference is zero, and along a finite path equality is transitive. This is the point representative needed below, not an assumption of independence of resolutions.

For the closure $C$ of a given height-one point, the prime-power costalk-reduction theorem supplies its finite normalization $\nu:\widetilde C\to C$: it is a universal homeomorphism and $\widetilde C$ is a strictly henselian trait. Apply embedded resolution to the union of $E$ and the strict transform of $C$; it suffices to blow up the nonregular or non-SNC points over $s$, since away from $s$ the strict transform is the single regular point $y$. Its final strict transform $C'$ is regular. The proper birational map $C'\to C$ factors through $\widetilde C$: on a normal affine chart, every element integral over the coordinate ring of $C$ lies in its integrally closed local rings in the common function field. This gives the factorization and its uniqueness by agreement on the generic point. The factor is proper since the normalization is separated, and is birational between reduced source and the normal one-dimensional trait target. Every point of the trait has codimension zero or a DVR local ring, so the modification-locus lemma makes this factor an isomorphism. Thus $C'=\widetilde C$, with a single closed point $z$ over $s$.

source.place: XVII §3.4.3, resolution adapted to a height-one closure

proof.text: Write $i:C\hookrightarrow S$, $i':C'\hookrightarrow S'$, $k:y\hookrightarrow U$, and $U'=S'-\{z\}$. Supported composition identifies cohomology supported at $s$ in $i^!\Lambda(2)$ with $H^4_s(S,\Lambda(2))$, and likewise at $z$ upstairs. The localization boundaries for these closed supports commute with forgetting support. On the common generic curve point, $k^!\Lambda(2)$ and the restriction of $i'{}^!\Lambda(2)$ agree by open restriction. Consequently the square comparing the maps from $H^3(y,k^!\Lambda(2))$ to $H^4_s(S,\Lambda(2))$ and $H^4_z(S',\Lambda(2))$, followed by enlargement to $E$, commutes: under supported composition its outer square is simply the square of restriction $H^3(U')\to H^3(U)$ with the maps forgetting the support $y$. Both routes are restriction from $U'$ to $U$ followed by forgetting support. This argument uses naturality of localization, not proper pullback of an exceptional functor along $p$.

Let $d=[\kappa(z):\kappa(s)]$. In the definition of the immediate transition along $y\rightsquigarrow s$, the transition on the normalization $C'$ is multiplied by $d^{-1}$. The first transition $\eta\rightsquigarrow y$ is computed on the strictly henselian DVR at $y$; the trait Gysin-residue theorem sends $1$ to the generic codimension-one Gysin class with its positive sign. On the regular trait $C'$ the second trait transition sends that class to $\operatorname{Cl}_{z\hookrightarrow C'}$ followed by the divisor Gysin class. Composition of regular-immersion classes is $\operatorname{Cl}_{z\hookrightarrow S'}$. The codimension-one classes given by the trait Gysin-residue theorem are absolute-purity classes of regular principal divisors on affine excellent regular neighbourhoods; by the Cartier-Gysin normalization they are the Kummer-normalized classes to which this composition rule applies, and step 8 identifies the composite with the absolute class. Thus the normalized two-step composite, through the commuting square of step 10, is enlargement of $d^{-1}\operatorname{Cl}_{z\hookrightarrow S'}$. This is $\epsilon(e_i)$ for any $D_i$ containing $z$, by step 8. The residue-degree comparison has precisely the factor $d$: for the finite radicial closed-point map, the prime-power Gysin class is multiplication by $d$. Hence its inverse is exactly the normalization in the definition, with no missing inseparable scalar. All these identifications respect the chosen geometric flags and strict-local restrictions. Apply finite residue-Gysin naturality to the finite normalization $C'\to C$ with coefficient $i^!\Lambda(1)$ and to the finite closed immersion $C\hookrightarrow S$; its generic comparison is the identity and its closed comparison is the degree-$d$ Gysin comparison. This is the comparison between the intrinsic trait transition and the ambient immediate transition used here.

source.place: XVII §3.4.3, final normalized diagram and cancellation of [z:s]

proof.text: Given two resolutions, form their fibre product over $S$ and take the reduced closure of the common generic point. This is an integral excellent Noetherian surface, projective over $S$, equal to $U$ away from the closed fibre. Apply the surface-resolution theorem, and then embedded resolution to its closed fibre. The resulting regular SNC resolution dominates both original ones. The morphisms to them are projective: the product projections are projective, and composition of projective morphisms is projective via the Segre embedding of the two projective-space factors. They are birational and their sources are reduced. Their targets are regular, hence normal; at codimension one their local rings are DVRs. The modification-locus lemma therefore gives an isomorphism open whose complement has dimension at most zero. The dominant closure is projective over the affine $S$, so the restricted $\mathcal O(1)$ is ample, as required by the resolution input; for the affine base $S$ itself, $\mathcal O_S$ is ample. To check dimension, normalize the dimension function on $S$ by $\delta(s)=0$. The finite-type formula has value $2$ at the generic point of the dominant closure and nonnegative values elsewhere, since residue transcendence degrees are nonnegative; its drops along chains give dimension at most $2$. The two-step chain specializing the generic point to a closed point of an exceptional curve gives dimension at least $2$. The projective embedding supplies the ample sheaf directly: the nonvanishing loci of homogeneous sections restrict to affine principal opens in the standard projective charts.

source.place: XVII §3.4.2, common domination and codimension-zero exceptional complement

proof.text: The complement of that isomorphism open cannot contain an exceptional curve, since each has dimension one. Its intersection with any exceptional curve is a proper closed subset of a Noetherian integral curve, hence finite. The remaining nonempty open contains a closed point: choose a nonempty affine open in it and a maximal ideal of its finite-type coordinate algebra; Zariski's lemma makes its residue field finite over $k$, so it is closed in the proper curve as well. Above such a point $z$ the dominating morphism has a unique point $z'$ with the same residue field. Restrict to the isomorphism neighbourhood of $z$. The open-restriction compatibility of the canonical regular-immersion class identifies $\operatorname{Cl}_{z\hookrightarrow S'}$ with $\operatorname{Cl}_{z'\hookrightarrow S''}$. The supported restriction triangle identifies these punctual supported groups with those on the neighbourhood. Enlarging support commutes with pullback by the functorial localization sequence. Since the residue degrees are equal, the normalized classes and their enlargements are equal as asserted.

source.place: XVII §3.4.2, closed point in the isomorphism locus and normalized Gysin comparison
